sources.citation: J. S. Feinstein, R. Adolphs, A. Damasio, D. Tranel (2011). The human amygdala and the induction and experience of fear. Current Biology.
sources.notes: Landmark behavioral study of Patient S.M. across snakes, spiders, Waverly Hills Haunted House, horror film clips, and 3 months of ecological momentary experience sampling.

sources.citation: J. S. Feinstein, C. Buzza, R. Hurlemann, R. L. Follmer et al. (2013). Fear and panic in humans with bilateral amygdala damage. Nature Neuroscience.
sources.notes: Single-breath 35% CO2 inhalation experiment in 3 bilateral amygdala lesion patients (S.M., A.M., B.G.) vs 12 healthy controls.

sources.citation: R. Adolphs, D. Tranel, H. Damasio, A. Damasio (1994). Impaired recognition of emotion in facial expressions following bilateral damage to the human amygdala. Nature.
sources.notes: Foundational Nature paper on Patient S.M. showing selective inability to recognize fear in human faces.

sources.citation: R. Adolphs, F. Gosselin, T. W. Buchanan, D. Tranel, P. Schyns, A. R. Damasio (2005). A mechanism for impaired fear recognition after amygdala damage. Nature.
sources.notes: Eye-tracking discovery that S.M. fails to look spontaneously at the eyes of fearful faces.

sources.citation: C. Tovote, J. P. Fadok, A. Lüthi (2015). Neuronal circuits for fear and anxiety. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.
sources.notes: Modern circuit synthesis distinguishing amygdala exteroceptive threat pathways from brainstem/insular interoceptive panic networks.

sources.citation: J. E. LeDoux, D. S. Pine (2016). Using neuroscience to help understand fear and anxiety: a two-system framework. American Journal of Psychiatry.
sources.notes: Two-system critique separating subcortical defensive survival circuits from cortical conscious feelings of fear and panic.
